lectures.title: Dialects, social variation and regional diversity

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
A conventional system of meaningful signs and rules used for communication and other mental and social activities.
questions.explanation:
A conventional system of meaningful signs and rules used for communication and other mental and social activities.
Example: Urdu speech and Pakistan Sign Language both organize meaningful signs through linguistic rules.
Key distinction: Natural signed languages demonstrate that language is not restricted to the vocal modality.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
Knowledge or use of one language, understood in relation to the definition and setting adopted.
questions.explanation:
Knowledge or use of one language, understood in relation to the definition and setting adopted.
Example: A person uses one language in everyday life while encountering several accents of it.
Key distinction: Dialect diversity within a language is distinguishable from using two named languages.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
Knowledge or use of two languages with potentially different abilities across tasks and settings.
questions.explanation:
Knowledge or use of two languages with potentially different abilities across tasks and settings.
Example: A student discusses family matters in Punjabi and writes university assignments in English.
Key distinction: A functional bilingual repertoire can be uneven and change with experience.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
Knowledge or use of more than one language; some teaching classifications reserve the term for three or more.
questions.explanation:
Knowledge or use of more than one language; some teaching classifications reserve the term for three or more.
Example: A learner uses Punjabi, Urdu and English for different purposes.
Key distinction: State the convention: broad usage includes bilingualism, while narrower classroom usage separates two from three or more.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
Knowledge or use of three languages.
questions.explanation:
Knowledge or use of three languages.
Example: A child has regular opportunities to communicate in English, Mandarin and Cantonese.
Key distinction: Exposure creates opportunities; proficiency depends on access, interaction and experience.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
A person who knows or uses several languages.
questions.explanation:
A person who knows or uses several languages.
Example: An adult communicates in several languages learned at different times.
Key distinction: It describes language repertoire rather than a diagnostic category or guaranteed cognitive trait.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
Acquisition of two languages from infancy or very early overlapping exposure.
questions.explanation:
Acquisition of two languages from infancy or very early overlapping exposure.
Example: A baby regularly interacts with caregivers in Urdu and Punjabi from birth.
Key distinction: Terminological age cutoffs vary, so describe actual exposure history rather than imposing a universal birthday boundary.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
Acquisition of an additional language after development in an earlier language has begun.
questions.explanation:
Acquisition of an additional language after development in an earlier language has begun.
Example: A Punjabi-speaking child begins regular Urdu interaction on entering preschool.
Key distinction: Successive and consecutive are commonly used for sequential acquisition; receptive ability is a different classification dimension.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
Bilingual development beginning during childhood.
questions.explanation:
Bilingual development beginning during childhood.
Example: A young child encounters a new community language after moving with the family.
Key distinction: Age of onset alone does not determine proficiency, maintenance or educational conditions.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
Bilingual development beginning relatively later than early childhood under a stated classification.
questions.explanation:
Bilingual development beginning relatively later than early childhood under a stated classification.
Example: A university student begins sustained use of a second language.
Key distinction: Age affects learning conditions and outcomes without making later bilingual development impossible.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
Understanding a language more extensively than one produces it.
questions.explanation:
Understanding a language more extensively than one produces it.
Example: A child understands a grandparent's Punjabi questions but usually answers in Urdu.
Key distinction: Receptive and expressive ability can differ because of opportunity, preference and proficiency.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
Ability to produce language through speaking, signing or writing in two languages.
questions.explanation:
Ability to produce language through speaking, signing or writing in two languages.
Example: A learner tells familiar stories in both Urdu and English.
Key distinction: Assess production directly and distinguish speaking, signing and writing demands.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
A profile in which one language is stronger overall or for particular tasks.
questions.explanation:
A profile in which one language is stronger overall or for particular tasks.
Example: A student reads English more easily but discusses family relationships more precisely in Urdu.
Key distinction: Dominance can differ by domain and change with education, migration and use.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
Relatively comparable proficiency in two languages under specified measures.
questions.explanation:
Relatively comparable proficiency in two languages under specified measures.
Example: Similar performance is observed in two languages on matched familiar communication tasks.
Key distinction: Balance is relative to tasks and measures, not complete mastery of two entire languages.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
Development of an additional language while the earlier language is supported and maintained.
questions.explanation:
Development of an additional language while the earlier language is supported and maintained.
Example: Urdu schooling is combined with meaningful Punjabi interaction and literacy opportunities.
Key distinction: Maintenance and support define the additive orientation; numerical balance is a separate issue.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
Development of a socially dominant language under conditions that erode an earlier language's use or development.
questions.explanation:
Development of a socially dominant language under conditions that erode an earlier language's use or development.
Example: A child stops using a stigmatized home language after sustained institutional pressure.
Key distinction: Loss is associated with social conditions and reduced support, not an unavoidable effect of bilingual learning.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
A language connected with family or community background that may differ from the dominant societal language.
questions.explanation:
A language connected with family or community background that may differ from the dominant societal language.
Example: A family maintains Punjabi during predominantly English schooling abroad.
Key distinction: Heritage affiliation, proficiency and literacy are distinct dimensions.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
A language with broad numerical or institutional dominance in a specified setting.
questions.explanation:
A language with broad numerical or institutional dominance in a specified setting.
Example: The language used in most local schooling receives extensive institutional support.
Key distinction: Specify the setting and distinguish social power from linguistic complexity.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
A language used by a numerically smaller or less institutionally powerful group in a stated context.
questions.explanation:
A language used by a numerically smaller or less institutionally powerful group in a stated context.
Example: A community language has few local school resources despite active home use.
Key distinction: Minority is a social relationship, not a judgment of linguistic capacity.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
A language acquired earliest, sometimes one of several acquired together.
questions.explanation:
A language acquired earliest, sometimes one of several acquired together.
Example: A child has two first languages because regular exposure to both began in infancy.
Key distinction: Acquisition order and current dominance must be recorded separately.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
A language learned or acquired beyond an existing repertoire.
questions.explanation:
A language learned or acquired beyond an existing repertoire.
Example: A student learns Arabic after developing Punjabi, Urdu and English.
Key distinction: In many contexts second language is a broad term; additional language avoids implying a precise numerical order.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
The set of linguistic resources a person can draw on across languages, varieties and modalities.
questions.explanation:
The set of linguistic resources a person can draw on across languages, varieties and modalities.
Example: A clinician documents home conversation, school writing and signed communication resources.
Key distinction: Repertoires are described through actual resources and practices, not nationality alone.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
A recurring social setting or activity associated with language choice.
questions.explanation:
A recurring social setting or activity associated with language choice.
Example: A family uses one language at home and another for university study.
Key distinction: Domains describe patterns of social use, such as home, work, education or worship.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
Understanding meaning conveyed through listening, reading or perceiving signed language.
questions.explanation:
Understanding meaning conveyed through listening, reading or perceiving signed language.
Example: A child follows a familiar signed instruction without producing the sign.
Key distinction: Understanding and production require related but distinguishable abilities.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
Production of meaningful language through speaking, signing or writing.
questions.explanation:
Production of meaningful language through speaking, signing or writing.
Example: A learner describes an event in a written paragraph.
Key distinction: Expression includes linguistic content and structure across modalities.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
Ability to read and write in two languages, with potentially uneven levels.
questions.explanation:
Ability to read and write in two languages, with potentially uneven levels.
Example: A student reads Urdu stories and writes English laboratory reports.
Key distinction: Literacy needs experience and instruction; oral bilingualism alone does not establish biliteracy.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
Bilingualism involving two languages in the same broad modality.
questions.explanation:
Bilingualism involving two languages in the same broad modality.
Example: A person uses spoken Punjabi and spoken Urdu.
Key distinction: Two spoken languages contrast with bimodal combinations involving different modalities.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
Bilingualism involving languages in different modalities, often signed and spoken.
questions.explanation:
Bilingualism involving languages in different modalities, often signed and spoken.
Example: A person uses Pakistan Sign Language and spoken Urdu.
Key distinction: Natural signed languages have their own linguistic organization and are not universal pantomime.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
Alternation between languages or varieties within an interaction or discourse.
questions.explanation:
Alternation between languages or varieties within an interaction or discourse.
Example: A speaker shifts from Urdu to English when quoting a lecturer.
Key distinction: Switching can be systematic and socially meaningful; definitions overlap with code-mixing across authors.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
A term often used for combining elements from different languages within an utterance.
questions.explanation:
A term often used for combining elements from different languages within an utterance.
Example: A speaker inserts an English technical noun into an otherwise Urdu sentence.
Key distinction: Terminology varies; identify the actual pattern and define the convention used.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
Incorporation of a form from another language into community usage, often with adaptation.
questions.explanation:
Incorporation of a form from another language into community usage, often with adaptation.
Example: A widely established loanword is pronounced with local sound patterns by many monolingual speakers.
Key distinction: Community integration can make a loanword part of a language's ordinary vocabulary.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
A perspective or practice emphasizing use of a multilingual person's integrated repertoire to make meaning.
questions.explanation:
A perspective or practice emphasizing use of a multilingual person's integrated repertoire to make meaning.
Example: Students discuss an idea using several resources before composing a report in the requested language.
Key distinction: Flexible repertoire use can coexist with explicit teaching of particular languages and genres.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
Effects of knowledge or use of one language on performance or development in another.
questions.explanation:
Effects of knowledge or use of one language on performance or development in another.
Example: A learner initially applies a familiar word-order pattern to a new language.
Key distinction: Influence can support learning or produce expected differences; direction and level matter.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
Continued use and transmission of a language despite pressure toward another.
questions.explanation:
Continued use and transmission of a language despite pressure toward another.
Example: Grandparents, caregivers and children sustain meaningful Punjabi conversation over time.
Key distinction: Relationships, access and sustained purposes support maintenance.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
A community or family's movement toward another language across time or generations.
questions.explanation:
A community or family's movement toward another language across time or generations.
Example: Younger generations increasingly use only the dominant school language.
Key distinction: Shift describes changing patterns of language use, often linked to power and transmission.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
Reduced accessibility or proficiency associated with changes such as diminished language use.
questions.explanation:
Reduced accessibility or proficiency associated with changes such as diminished language use.
Example: An adult retrieves less-used words less readily after years in another language environment.
Key distinction: Reduced accessibility can be selective and may change with renewed use.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
Ability to reflect on language forms, meanings and conventions as objects of thought.
questions.explanation:
Ability to reflect on language forms, meanings and conventions as objects of thought.
Example: A child notices that two different words can name the same object across languages.
Key distinction: It concerns reflection on language rather than volume, and varies with task and experience.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
Research evaluating whether bilingual experience is associated with differences in cognitive performance.
questions.explanation:
Research evaluating whether bilingual experience is associated with differences in cognitive performance.
Example: A study compares carefully matched groups on one attention task and reports uncertainty.
Key distinction: Findings depend on tasks and populations; broad cognitive superiority is not an established universal outcome.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
Knowledge spread across languages because experiences and contexts differ.
questions.explanation:
Knowledge spread across languages because experiences and contexts differ.
Example: A child knows kitchen items mainly in Punjabi and classroom terms mainly in English.
Key distinction: Sample relevant languages and contexts before drawing conclusions from a single-language vocabulary test.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
A record of exposure, acquisition, use, schooling and change across the person's languages.
questions.explanation:
A record of exposure, acquisition, use, schooling and change across the person's languages.
Example: An interview asks who uses each language, when regular exposure began and where it occurs.
Key distinction: A detailed profile is more informative than a binary monolingual-versus-bilingual label alone.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
A contested deficit label historically applied to apparently limited performance in two languages.
questions.explanation:
A contested deficit label historically applied to apparently limited performance in two languages.
Example: A reviewer replaces a broad deficit label with a detailed profile of opportunity, skills and language needs.
Key distinction: The handout lists vocabulary, grammatical accuracy, processing, creativity, functions and imagery; assess these specifically rather than assuming a deficient person.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which term matches the following description?
A distinction between oral sound production and the broader organization and use of a linguistic system.
questions.explanation:
A distinction between oral sound production and the broader organization and use of a linguistic system.
Example: A person can have language competence through signing without producing speech.
Key distinction: Evaluate modality and the relevant communication system rather than equating speech with language.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Identify the concept defined below.
Knowledge or use of multiple languages by a particular person.
questions.explanation:
Knowledge or use of multiple languages by a particular person.
Example: One student uses three languages across home, study and work.
Key distinction: Individual repertoires and societal language diversity are distinct levels of description.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question:
Which concept is described here?
Presence and use of multiple languages within a society or institution.
questions.explanation:
Presence and use of multiple languages within a society or institution.
Example: A city contains several language communities and multilingual institutions.
Key distinction: A society can be multilingual while some members use only one language.
questions.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

questions.question: Which additional evidence is most necessary before treating an apparent benefit on one inhibition task as a general bilingual advantage?
options: A single successful participant described in an anecdote
Replication across relevant tasks and populations with careful control of confounds
The fact that the bilingual group speaks a prestigious language
A statement that bilingual participants are culturally interesting
questions.explanation: A narrow task result supports a narrow inference. Broader claims require appropriate comparisons, replication and attention to age, education, experience and publication bias. Valuable communication and social benefits do not require universal superiority on executive-function tasks.

questions.question: A speaker uses English technical terms in an Urdu sentence. Which observation would most help distinguish a momentary bilingual insertion from an established community loanword?

Whether the speaker says the word loudly
Whether English has official status in another country
Whether the utterance contains a question mark
questions.explanation: Borrowing concerns incorporation into a community repertoire, while switching or mixing concerns multilingual alternation under a specified analytic convention. Conventionalization, adaptation and distribution provide evidence; one isolated token may not settle the classification.

questions.question: A child has low English naming scores after brief English exposure, communicates effectively in Punjabi and learns new labels readily with support. What is the best immediate interpretation?
options: English scores alone establish a disorder in every language
Limited English opportunity is a plausible contributor; gather a broader profile before diagnosis
The family should stop Punjabi before further assessment
Good learning response conclusively rules out all developmental concerns
questions.explanation: Exposure history, home-language functioning and learning response make a language difference plausible. They do not independently provide a final diagnosis. Combine language samples, caregiver information, hearing and developmental history, appropriate measures and follow-up as indicated.
questions.referenceSection: Original hypothetical case connecting the supplied lecture topics with the Reading guide.

questions.question: Which plan best distinguishes cross-language transfer from improvement only on practiced material?
options: Ask whether the child likes the clinician and infer grammatical transfer
Record only the number of worksheets completed
Repeat the identical trained item once and infer transfer to both languages
Probe untrained targets in both the trained and untrained languages at planned times
questions.explanation: Separate trained-item learning, within-language generalization and cross-language change. Planned probes in each relevant language help show where improvement occurs. Functional observations with relevant partners also matter; transfer should not be assumed.

questions.question: Which task is both cognitively demanding and relatively context-embedded?
options: Explaining competing predictions while manipulating a visible experiment
Repeating a known greeting without visual cues
Copying a familiar label from a board without interpreting it
Reciting one memorized word in an empty room
questions.explanation: Comparing predictions requires reasoning, while the visible experiment supplies contextual cues. Cognitive demand and contextual support are separate dimensions. Strong support need not mean simplistic content.

questions.question: A child has been quiet in a new school language for seven months. What follows from the handout’s six-month silent-period description?
options: Seven months automatically establishes selective mutism
It is not a diagnostic deadline; review exposure, participation and broader development
The child must be ignored until exactly five years have elapsed
The family should be instructed to eliminate the home language
questions.explanation: Stage timings are broad teaching approximations rather than validated diagnostic cutoffs. Examine comprehension, accessible interaction, home-language communication, anxiety, hearing and developmental concerns. Persistent or concerning patterns deserve appropriate assessment; a stage label should not justify indefinite waiting.

questions.question: Which comparison correctly distinguishes an idiom, a proverb and a euphemism?
options: An idiom has conventional nonliteral meaning; a proverb offers general wisdom; a euphemism softens reference
All three are diagnostic signs of language confusion
An idiom is a regional accent; a proverb is a test score; a euphemism is always an insult
An idiom softens every topic; a proverb must be literal; a euphemism has no audience
questions.explanation: These categories describe different functions and can sometimes overlap in particular expressions. Idiomatic meaning is not fully predictable word by word; a proverb conveys a conventional observation or lesson; euphemistic wording manages sensitivity. Interpretation still depends on context.

questions.question: A child uses a negative-concord pattern also used by fluent community members. What should an SLP establish before labeling it a grammatical impairment?
options: Whether the form is systematic and appropriate in the child’s variety and what other evidence shows
Whether the child can suppress all home-language identity markers
Whether the child’s family belongs to a prestigious occupation
Whether the standard written variety forbids the form, as the sole diagnostic criterion
questions.explanation: Dialect-specific grammatical patterns are not impairment merely because a school standard differs. Describe distribution within the relevant variety and examine the wider language profile. Teaching institutional writing conventions is distinguishable from diagnosing disorder.
questions.referenceSection: Original hypothetical case connecting the supplied lecture topics with the Reading guide.

questions.question: Which conclusion about the lecture’s lists of gender, food and religious practices is defensible?
options: They prove that every listed practice is prohibited in every society
They show that one cultural group has no internal diversity
They diagnose communication preferences from nationality alone
They prompt contextual inquiry and cannot establish every individual’s behavior
questions.explanation: Practices differ across individuals, settings, communities and time. Lists are starting points for respectful inquiry, not universal behavioral laws. Ask what matters in the actual encounter and distinguish a social description from a religious or legal claim.

concepts.definition: A conventional system of meaningful signs and rules used for communication and other mental and social activities.
concepts.example: Urdu speech and Pakistan Sign Language both organize meaningful signs through linguistic rules.
concepts.false: A system must use sound to qualify as a language.
concepts.note: Natural signed languages demonstrate that language is not restricted to the vocal modality.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Knowledge or use of one language, understood in relation to the definition and setting adopted.
concepts.example: A person uses one language in everyday life while encountering several accents of it.
concepts.false: Speaking different dialects necessarily makes a person bilingual.
concepts.note: Dialect diversity within a language is distinguishable from using two named languages.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Knowledge or use of two languages with potentially different abilities across tasks and settings.
concepts.example: A student discusses family matters in Punjabi and writes university assignments in English.
concepts.false: Bilingual status requires identical scores in every skill in both languages.
concepts.note: A functional bilingual repertoire can be uneven and change with experience.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Knowledge or use of more than one language; some teaching classifications reserve the term for three or more.
concepts.example: A learner uses Punjabi, Urdu and English for different purposes.
concepts.false: Multilingual always means exactly three equally fluent spoken languages.
concepts.note: State the convention: broad usage includes bilingualism, while narrower classroom usage separates two from three or more.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Knowledge or use of three languages.
concepts.example: A child has regular opportunities to communicate in English, Mandarin and Cantonese.
concepts.false: Merely hearing three language names guarantees active command of all three.
concepts.note: Exposure creates opportunities; proficiency depends on access, interaction and experience.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A person who knows or uses several languages.
concepts.example: An adult communicates in several languages learned at different times.
concepts.false: Polyglot is a clinical diagnosis of unusually high intelligence.
concepts.note: It describes language repertoire rather than a diagnostic category or guaranteed cognitive trait.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Acquisition of two languages from infancy or very early overlapping exposure.
concepts.example: A baby regularly interacts with caregivers in Urdu and Punjabi from birth.
concepts.false: Simultaneous acquisition means successive acquisition beginning in adulthood.
concepts.note: Terminological age cutoffs vary, so describe actual exposure history rather than imposing a universal birthday boundary.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Acquisition of an additional language after development in an earlier language has begun.
concepts.example: A Punjabi-speaking child begins regular Urdu interaction on entering preschool.
concepts.false: Sequential and successive acquisition are unrelated processes.
concepts.note: Successive and consecutive are commonly used for sequential acquisition; receptive ability is a different classification dimension.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Bilingual development beginning during childhood.
concepts.example: A young child encounters a new community language after moving with the family.
concepts.false: Early bilingualism guarantees equal proficiency and additive outcomes.
concepts.note: Age of onset alone does not determine proficiency, maintenance or educational conditions.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Bilingual development beginning relatively later than early childhood under a stated classification.
concepts.example: A university student begins sustained use of a second language.
concepts.false: Adults cannot become bilingual after the early childhood period.
concepts.note: Age affects learning conditions and outcomes without making later bilingual development impossible.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Understanding a language more extensively than one produces it.
concepts.example: A child understands a grandparent's Punjabi questions but usually answers in Urdu.
concepts.false: Understanding without speaking necessarily indicates a speech-language disorder.
concepts.note: Receptive and expressive ability can differ because of opportunity, preference and proficiency.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Ability to produce language through speaking, signing or writing in two languages.
concepts.example: A learner tells familiar stories in both Urdu and English.
concepts.false: Productive ability can be inferred solely from a listening score.
concepts.note: Assess production directly and distinguish speaking, signing and writing demands.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A profile in which one language is stronger overall or for particular tasks.
concepts.example: A student reads English more easily but discusses family relationships more precisely in Urdu.
concepts.false: A person's dominant language is fixed permanently by the language first heard.
concepts.note: Dominance can differ by domain and change with education, migration and use.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Relatively comparable proficiency in two languages under specified measures.
concepts.example: Similar performance is observed in two languages on matched familiar communication tasks.
concepts.false: Balanced bilingualism means perfect knowledge of every word in both languages.
concepts.note: Balance is relative to tasks and measures, not complete mastery of two entire languages.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Development of an additional language while the earlier language is supported and maintained.
concepts.example: Urdu schooling is combined with meaningful Punjabi interaction and literacy opportunities.
concepts.false: Additive bilingualism requires exactly equal proficiency in both languages.
concepts.note: Maintenance and support define the additive orientation; numerical balance is a separate issue.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Development of a socially dominant language under conditions that erode an earlier language's use or development.
concepts.example: A child stops using a stigmatized home language after sustained institutional pressure.
concepts.false: Learning a new language inevitably damages the earlier language.
concepts.note: Loss is associated with social conditions and reduced support, not an unavoidable effect of bilingual learning.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A language connected with family or community background that may differ from the dominant societal language.
concepts.example: A family maintains Punjabi during predominantly English schooling abroad.
concepts.false: A heritage language must be the person's strongest written language.
concepts.note: Heritage affiliation, proficiency and literacy are distinct dimensions.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A language with broad numerical or institutional dominance in a specified setting.
concepts.example: The language used in most local schooling receives extensive institutional support.
concepts.false: Majority status proves that a language has a superior grammar.
concepts.note: Specify the setting and distinguish social power from linguistic complexity.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A language used by a numerically smaller or less institutionally powerful group in a stated context.
concepts.example: A community language has few local school resources despite active home use.
concepts.false: Minority status means the language has fewer expressive possibilities.
concepts.note: Minority is a social relationship, not a judgment of linguistic capacity.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A language acquired earliest, sometimes one of several acquired together.
concepts.example: A child has two first languages because regular exposure to both began in infancy.
concepts.false: Every person has exactly one first language that remains strongest forever.
concepts.note: Acquisition order and current dominance must be recorded separately.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A language learned or acquired beyond an existing repertoire.
concepts.example: A student learns Arabic after developing Punjabi, Urdu and English.
concepts.false: The label second language always means the learner has only two languages.
concepts.note: In many contexts second language is a broad term; additional language avoids implying a precise numerical order.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The set of linguistic resources a person can draw on across languages, varieties and modalities.
concepts.example: A clinician documents home conversation, school writing and signed communication resources.
concepts.false: A repertoire is fully represented by the person's passport nationality.
concepts.note: Repertoires are described through actual resources and practices, not nationality alone.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A recurring social setting or activity associated with language choice.
concepts.example: A family uses one language at home and another for university study.
concepts.false: A home language domain is a separate grammar organ in the brain.
concepts.note: Domains describe patterns of social use, such as home, work, education or worship.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Understanding meaning conveyed through listening, reading or perceiving signed language.
concepts.example: A child follows a familiar signed instruction without producing the sign.
concepts.false: Receptive knowledge is identical to the ability to name the same item.
concepts.note: Understanding and production require related but distinguishable abilities.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Production of meaningful language through speaking, signing or writing.
concepts.example: A learner describes an event in a written paragraph.
concepts.false: Expressive language refers only to emotional tone of voice.
concepts.note: Expression includes linguistic content and structure across modalities.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Ability to read and write in two languages, with potentially uneven levels.
concepts.example: A student reads Urdu stories and writes English laboratory reports.
concepts.false: Speaking two languages automatically establishes literacy in both scripts.
concepts.note: Literacy needs experience and instruction; oral bilingualism alone does not establish biliteracy.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Bilingualism involving two languages in the same broad modality.
concepts.example: A person uses spoken Punjabi and spoken Urdu.
concepts.false: Using a spoken and a signed language is unimodal bilingualism.
concepts.note: Two spoken languages contrast with bimodal combinations involving different modalities.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Bilingualism involving languages in different modalities, often signed and spoken.
concepts.example: A person uses Pakistan Sign Language and spoken Urdu.
concepts.false: A signed language is merely a silent version of the local spoken language.
concepts.note: Natural signed languages have their own linguistic organization and are not universal pantomime.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Alternation between languages or varieties within an interaction or discourse.
concepts.example: A speaker shifts from Urdu to English when quoting a lecturer.
concepts.false: Switching language demonstrates that a bilingual has no grammatical knowledge.
concepts.note: Switching can be systematic and socially meaningful; definitions overlap with code-mixing across authors.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A term often used for combining elements from different languages within an utterance.
concepts.example: A speaker inserts an English technical noun into an otherwise Urdu sentence.
concepts.false: Code-mixing has a universally agreed boundary excluding all within-sentence code-switching.
concepts.note: Terminology varies; identify the actual pattern and define the convention used.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Incorporation of a form from another language into community usage, often with adaptation.
concepts.example: A widely established loanword is pronounced with local sound patterns by many monolingual speakers.
concepts.false: Any established loanword proves that its current speaker is bilingual.
concepts.note: Community integration can make a loanword part of a language's ordinary vocabulary.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A perspective or practice emphasizing use of a multilingual person's integrated repertoire to make meaning.
concepts.example: Students discuss an idea using several resources before composing a report in the requested language.
concepts.false: Translanguaging means abandoning every learning objective or audience requirement.
concepts.note: Flexible repertoire use can coexist with explicit teaching of particular languages and genres.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Effects of knowledge or use of one language on performance or development in another.
concepts.example: A learner initially applies a familiar word-order pattern to a new language.
concepts.false: Influence between languages is always evidence of neurological impairment.
concepts.note: Influence can support learning or produce expected differences; direction and level matter.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Continued use and transmission of a language despite pressure toward another.
concepts.example: Grandparents, caregivers and children sustain meaningful Punjabi conversation over time.
concepts.false: A language is maintained by displaying its name without opportunities to use it.
concepts.note: Relationships, access and sustained purposes support maintenance.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A community or family's movement toward another language across time or generations.
concepts.example: Younger generations increasingly use only the dominant school language.
concepts.false: Language shift is the same as one individual briefly forgetting a word.
concepts.note: Shift describes changing patterns of language use, often linked to power and transmission.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Reduced accessibility or proficiency associated with changes such as diminished language use.
concepts.example: An adult retrieves less-used words less readily after years in another language environment.
concepts.false: Attrition necessarily means every trace of the language has been erased.
concepts.note: Reduced accessibility can be selective and may change with renewed use.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Ability to reflect on language forms, meanings and conventions as objects of thought.
concepts.example: A child notices that two different words can name the same object across languages.
concepts.false: Metalinguistic awareness is simply loud or confident speech.
concepts.note: It concerns reflection on language rather than volume, and varies with task and experience.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Research evaluating whether bilingual experience is associated with differences in cognitive performance.
concepts.example: A study compares carefully matched groups on one attention task and reports uncertainty.
concepts.false: Bilingualism guarantees superior intelligence and executive functioning in every individual.
concepts.note: Findings depend on tasks and populations; broad cognitive superiority is not an established universal outcome.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Knowledge spread across languages because experiences and contexts differ.
concepts.example: A child knows kitchen items mainly in Punjabi and classroom terms mainly in English.
concepts.false: A lower score in one language fully measures the child's total conceptual knowledge.
concepts.note: Sample relevant languages and contexts before drawing conclusions from a single-language vocabulary test.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A record of exposure, acquisition, use, schooling and change across the person's languages.
concepts.example: An interview asks who uses each language, when regular exposure began and where it occurs.
concepts.false: A single bilingual label replaces the need to investigate actual experience.
concepts.note: A detailed profile is more informative than a binary monolingual-versus-bilingual label alone.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: An unsupported generalization that treats bilingual learning itself as a cause of disorder or confusion.
concepts.example: A teacher blames two languages for every communication difficulty without assessment.
concepts.false: Reducing a child's languages is the standard cure for language disorder.
concepts.note: Multilingual development and communication disorder require separate consideration and individualized evidence.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A variation explained by language, dialect or learning experience rather than impairment.
concepts.example: A learner uses an expected home-language pattern while acquiring English.
concepts.false: A difference from monolingual English is sufficient evidence of disorder.
concepts.note: Compare the pattern with appropriate linguistic and experiential expectations.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Persistent difficulty learning or using language that cannot be explained solely by limited opportunity to learn a particular language.
concepts.example: Concerns persist across the child's linguistic repertoire after opportunities and contexts are considered.
concepts.false: Any low score in the newest language establishes a language disorder.
concepts.note: Multilingual manifestations can differ across languages; evaluate the full profile rather than requiring identical errors.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Opportunities to hear, see and interact through a language over time.
concepts.example: A clinician records conversations, school use and accessible signed input.
concepts.false: The percentage of exposure alone determines whether a child has a disorder.
concepts.note: Consider quality, accessibility, interaction, duration and changing needs together.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Communication that follows the learner's focus and responds meaningfully to their attempts.
concepts.example: A caregiver expands a child's comment during shared play.
concepts.false: Passive background television provides the same interaction as responsive conversation.
concepts.note: Contingent exchanges create opportunities to understand and use language meaningfully.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Sustaining family language communication while additional languages develop.
concepts.example: Parents share stories naturally in the language they use most comfortably.
concepts.false: Parents must stop their strongest language to make school-language learning possible.
concepts.note: Family communication and relationships are important; a blanket home-language ban is not an evidence-based default.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A family language arrangement in which particular people usually use particular languages.
concepts.example: One caregiver usually uses Urdu and another usually uses Punjabi.
concepts.false: Every bilingual family must use one person per language to avoid confusion.
concepts.note: This is one possible arrangement, not a requirement or guarantee of balanced development.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A family strategy giving the less socially supported language sustained home use.
concepts.example: A family uses Punjabi at home while school provides extensive English exposure.
concepts.false: The home strategy alone guarantees equal reading skill in both languages.
concepts.note: Outcomes depend on meaningful access, interaction and literacy opportunities beyond a label.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: An exchange drawing on more than one language.
concepts.example: A child combines languages while talking with a relative who shares both.
concepts.false: A mixed utterance is a diagnostic sign of language confusion.
concepts.note: Interpret mixing through the speaker's resources, audience and communicative purpose.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The tendency for bilingual people to develop and use languages for different purposes, people and settings.
concepts.example: A worker uses technical English at work and family Urdu at home.
concepts.false: A bilingual should be assessed as two complete monolinguals with identical experiences.
concepts.note: Domain-specific experience helps explain uneven vocabulary and proficiency.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Collaborative selection of languages and delivery arrangements to meet communication needs.
concepts.example: An SLP and family prioritize meaningful goals in Urdu and Punjabi with appropriate support.
concepts.false: The clinician's easiest language automatically overrides every family communication need.
concepts.note: Include language history, client priorities, available expertise and appropriate collaboration.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: An approach targeting shared underlying skills or features relevant across the client's languages.
concepts.example: Therapy develops narrative organization used in both home and school communication.
concepts.false: A bilingual approach requires assuming that every language has identical grammatical forms.
concepts.note: Shared goals do not erase language-specific structures or differences in expression.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: An approach addressing features and needs specific to particular languages as well as their relationships.
concepts.example: A clinician plans separate targets for sounds or grammatical forms that differ between Urdu and English.
concepts.false: A cross-linguistic approach treats every difference between languages as an error.
concepts.note: Identify relevant contrasts and select targets appropriate to each language system.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A relevant property present in more than one of the client's languages.
concepts.example: A sound occurs in the inventories of both languages under assessment.
concepts.false: A shared sound must have exactly the same distribution and acquisition history in both languages.
concepts.note: Compare phonetic realization, word position and linguistic context before assuming equivalence.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Comparison of language or dialect systems to identify relevant similarities and differences.
concepts.example: An SLP checks whether a target grammatical marking exists in the home language.
concepts.false: A home-language difference should be corrected as a disorder without comparison.
concepts.note: Contrastive information supports interpretation but does not replace individual assessment.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Change in an untrained language following learning or intervention in another.
concepts.example: An SLP probes home-language narrative organization after school-language narrative work.
concepts.false: Successful transfer should be assumed without measuring the untrained language.
concepts.note: Generalization varies with targets and experience and should be monitored directly.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Extension of learning to untrained items or situations within the same language.
concepts.example: A newly practiced sound appears in untrained Urdu words.
concepts.false: Transfer to a new Urdu word is necessarily transfer to a second language.
concepts.note: Specify whether the change crosses items, settings, partners or languages.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Teaching meaning that can be connected with language-specific labels and expressions.
concepts.example: The idea of clothing categories is explored using familiar items and words in both languages.
concepts.false: Vocabulary teaching is unnecessary whenever concepts are addressed.
concepts.note: Concepts and vocabulary are complementary; teach useful labels and structures as goals require.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Words and expressions selected for usefulness in the person's everyday activities.
concepts.example: A child practices requesting preferred food and asking for help at school.
concepts.false: Only grammatical structure matters in bilingual intervention.
concepts.note: Meaningful vocabulary can support participation alongside syntax, speech and discourse goals.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Support for organizing and expressing connected accounts or stories.
concepts.example: A child practices characters, a problem and an outcome using familiar events.
concepts.false: One story style is universally appropriate across all cultural communities.
concepts.note: Story tasks and expectations should be adapted to linguistic and cultural experience.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A recurring meaningful phrase or structure that provides repeated practice.
concepts.example: Shared play repeatedly models a request structure with different desired objects.
concepts.false: Repetition is useful only when meaning and participation are removed.
concepts.note: Repeated structure is most informative when the learner understands its communicative purpose.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Selection of activities that connect language goals with the learner's interests.
concepts.example: A child interested in buses describes routes and asks for missing items.
concepts.false: Interest-based work means abandoning measurable communication goals.
concepts.note: Motivation supports practice while goals and progress remain explicit.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Collaborative support helping caregivers use feasible communication strategies in everyday routines.
concepts.example: An SLP models expansions during shared book time and asks what fits family life.
concepts.false: Sending an untranslated worksheet is sufficient evidence of caregiver coaching.
concepts.note: Check understanding, language accessibility and feasibility through respectful collaboration.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Agreed opportunities to apply communication targets between sessions.
concepts.example: A family chooses a brief story routine compatible with its schedule.
concepts.false: Missed homework proves that the family does not value communication.
concepts.note: Discuss time, literacy, materials and access before attributing participation to motivation.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Repeated measurement of relevant performance during intervention.
concepts.example: The clinician checks target use in both languages and everyday settings.
concepts.false: Improvement during one rehearsed activity establishes broad functional progress.
concepts.note: Use planned probes and functional information to distinguish practice effects from wider change.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: An initial measure of a target before the relevant intervention phase.
concepts.example: Familiar and untrained words are sampled before a new speech target is taught.
concepts.false: A baseline should be collected only after the target has been mastered.
concepts.note: Initial performance provides a reference for evaluating later change.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Collection and analysis of representative communication in meaningful contexts.
concepts.example: A clinician gathers conversation and narrative samples across the child's languages with support as needed.
concepts.false: A short naming list represents all aspects of conversational competence.
concepts.note: Samples should cover appropriate partners, tasks and linguistic contexts.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Assessment of learning potential and response to supported teaching, often using test-teach-retest.
concepts.example: A learner is taught a novel narrative strategy and then assessed for transfer.
concepts.false: Dynamic assessment is simply repeating the same test without teaching or observation.
concepts.note: Examine the support required and learning response alongside other assessment evidence.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Responsiveness to mediation and the effort needed to support learning during dynamic assessment.
concepts.example: A child rapidly applies a strategy after a brief demonstration.
concepts.false: High modifiability alone conclusively rules out every communication disorder.
concepts.note: Learning response is useful evidence within a broader assessment, not an isolated diagnostic verdict.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Counting a concept once when it is known in either language.
concepts.example: Knowing both the Urdu and English labels for one object contributes one concept.
concepts.false: Translation equivalents count as two separate concepts in conceptual scoring.
concepts.note: Conceptual counts distinguish unique meanings from the number of language-specific word forms known.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Counting known word forms across languages, with translation equivalents counted separately.
concepts.example: A child knows 20 Urdu labels and 15 English labels, giving 35 word forms.
concepts.false: Total vocabulary scoring subtracts every translation equivalent.
concepts.note: State the scoring convention and do not confuse word-form totals with unique concept counts.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Interpretation against reference data suited to the individual and assessment purpose.
concepts.example: A clinician checks whether a test's standardization includes a comparable linguistic population.
concepts.false: Translating an English test preserves its original standard scores automatically.
concepts.note: Translation changes item and administration properties; standardized interpretations require supporting validity evidence.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A trained professional supporting communication across spoken or signed languages.
concepts.example: An SLP briefs an interpreter before an assessment and discusses linguistic observations afterward.
concepts.false: An interpreter independently replaces the SLP's clinical responsibility.
concepts.note: The clinician retains responsibility while collaborating within each professional's competence.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A professional rendering written content from one language into another.
concepts.example: A family information sheet is translated and checked for clarity.
concepts.false: Written translation and live spoken interpretation are identical tasks.
concepts.note: Distinguish the modality and skills needed for the particular communication task.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A collaborator helping explain relevant cultural practices and meanings across participants.
concepts.example: A broker helps the team understand a family's expectations about an assessment meeting.
concepts.false: A cultural broker can speak for the preferences of every person in a community.
concepts.note: Community knowledge supports dialogue but does not replace asking the individual family.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Assessment of hearing access as one relevant contributor to communication concerns.
concepts.example: A child with concerns in several settings is referred for appropriate hearing evaluation.
concepts.false: Every difficulty in a bilingual child can be explained by bilingual exposure.
concepts.note: Consider hearing and developmental history rather than attributing all concerns to language learning.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: An outcome framed around communication in a valued life activity.
concepts.example: A child can request clarification from a teacher and communicate needs to grandparents.
concepts.false: Correct worksheet responses automatically establish participation in every setting.
concepts.note: Measure communication where it matters, with relevant partners and languages.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A plan developed with the client and family around their priorities, resources and informed preferences.
concepts.example: The team asks which languages are needed for caregiving and school participation.
concepts.false: The majority language is automatically the family's only legitimate priority.
concepts.note: Decisions should respect the actual communication ecology and available evidence.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Adjustment of communication or task conditions to improve access while preserving the intended goal.
concepts.example: An SLP uses accessible pictures and clarified instructions to make a task understandable.
concepts.false: Accommodation requires the family to abandon its language and cultural identity.
concepts.note: Explain what is adjusted and document any implications for test interpretation.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Adoption of practices of a dominant group, sometimes involving pressure to relinquish earlier practices.
concepts.example: A child faces pressure to give up the home language to fit school expectations.
concepts.false: Assimilation and accessible accommodation are the same clinical process.
concepts.note: Distinguish adapting access from requiring cultural or linguistic replacement.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Development of knowledge and use of a language beyond an earlier language.
concepts.example: A school learner gradually understands and uses English after early Urdu exposure.
concepts.false: Additional-language development proceeds independently of context and opportunity.
concepts.note: Exposure, interaction, instruction, prior knowledge and learner circumstances shape development.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A teaching description of early additional-language learning with limited overt production.
concepts.example: A new learner watches a task, understands some routines and communicates by pointing.
concepts.false: A pre-production description implies that the child understands nothing.
concepts.note: Receptive skills and nonverbal participation may precede extensive production.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A period of reduced production in a newly encountered language while other communication may continue.
concepts.example: A child speaks freely at home but initially listens more in the new school language.
concepts.false: Every silent period lasts exactly six months and requires no monitoring.
concepts.note: Duration and behavior vary; persistent concerns require contextual review rather than a fixed waiting rule.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A teaching description in which learners use short, often one- or two-word additional-language responses.
concepts.example: A learner answers a supported choice question with a short phrase.
concepts.false: Short early responses show that the learner is incapable of complex thought.
concepts.note: Limited expression in a new language should not be confused with limited reasoning.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A teaching description of increasing use of phrases and simple sentences with continuing errors.
concepts.example: A child explains a familiar classroom activity using short sentences.
concepts.false: Expected developmental errors during speech emergence establish a language disorder.
concepts.note: Compare errors with exposure and the learner's broader language profile.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A teaching description of increasingly complex communication that still needs language support.
concepts.example: A learner joins a discussion but asks for clarification of abstract terms.
concepts.false: Conversational participation at this stage makes clarification unnecessary.
concepts.note: Complexity, genre and familiarity can still create substantial demands.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A teaching description of effective additional-language use across increasingly demanding contexts.
concepts.example: A student communicates effectively but still learns unfamiliar disciplinary expressions.
concepts.false: Advanced fluency means no future vocabulary or genre learning is needed.
concepts.note: Proficiency remains task-dependent and continues to develop with use.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Recognition that broad acquisition-stage descriptions are instructional guides rather than universal diagnostic sequences.
concepts.example: A learner produces complex rehearsed language but needs help in an unfamiliar task.
concepts.false: Every learner must match the same vocabulary total at the same elapsed month.
concepts.note: Fixed word counts and timelines should not be treated as validated individual milestones.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Cummins's term for skills involved in everyday interpersonal communication, often supported by context.
concepts.example: A student chats with classmates while seeing the objects and actions discussed.
concepts.false: BICS describes the complete set of abilities needed for academic success.
concepts.note: Familiar conversation can mask difficulty with the language demands of curriculum tasks.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Cummins's term emphasizing language proficiency needed for cognitively demanding academic learning.
concepts.example: A learner explains evidence in an expository paragraph using precise relationships.
concepts.false: CALP is a separate language stored independently of everyday communication.
concepts.note: This is a conceptual distinction about demands and proficiency, not two isolated language organs.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Cummins's proposal that some knowledge and skills can support performance across languages.
concepts.example: Understanding narrative sequence in one language supports learning to express it in another.
concepts.false: CUP predicts automatic transfer of every grammatical form without exposure.
concepts.note: Shared resources can support learning while surface forms and transfer conditions remain important.
