concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: An illustration of distinct language surface forms with some shared underlying resources.
concepts.example: Two visible peaks represent languages above a shared base of knowledge.
concepts.false: The iceberg picture is a literal anatomical map of the bilingual brain.
concepts.note: The image is a conceptual teaching metaphor, not a claim that languages are physically fused.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Communication supported by visible, shared or interactional cues.
concepts.example: A teacher demonstrates an action while naming it and checking understanding.
concepts.false: Contextual support necessarily makes the intellectual content trivial.
concepts.note: Context support and cognitive demand are separate dimensions.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Communication with fewer immediate situational cues to aid interpretation.
concepts.example: A learner reads an unfamiliar abstract argument without a demonstration.
concepts.false: Written communication is always equally context-reduced regardless of pictures or prior knowledge.
concepts.note: Cues, familiarity and interaction alter support in both spoken and written activities.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The reasoning, memory and conceptual work a task requires.
concepts.example: Comparing two explanations requires more reasoning than repeating an already understood label.
concepts.false: The number of unfamiliar words alone fully determines cognitive demand.
concepts.note: Linguistic difficulty and conceptual demand interact but should be distinguished.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A framework examining contextual support and cognitive demand together.
concepts.example: A complex science demonstration offers strong visual support despite demanding reasoning.
concepts.false: A cognitively demanding task must remove all contextual support.
concepts.note: Support can preserve conceptual challenge while increasing language access.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Temporary, responsive support adjusted as the learner gains control.
concepts.example: A teacher models one explanation, uses prompts and gradually reduces them.
concepts.false: Scaffolding means completing every task for the learner indefinitely.
concepts.note: Effective support enables increasing participation and independence.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Pictures, objects or demonstrations that make relevant meaning more accessible.
concepts.example: A sequence of images helps a learner explain an event.
concepts.false: Pictures automatically have the same meaning for every cultural audience.
concepts.note: Check interpretation and relevance rather than assuming visual universality.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Language input made sufficiently understandable through its relation to knowledge and contextual support.
concepts.example: A teacher uses familiar ideas, demonstration and manageable language for a new concept.
concepts.false: Hearing uninterpretable language for long periods ensures comprehension.
concepts.note: Access to meaning matters; input is one contribution within an interactive learning environment.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Exchanges in which participants respond to meaning and work toward a communication purpose.
concepts.example: Partners ask and answer questions to locate a missing picture.
concepts.false: Interaction is equivalent to repeating unrelated sounds without a communicative aim.
concepts.note: Reciprocal communication creates opportunities for understanding, expression and feedback.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Interactional work to resolve a problem in understanding.
concepts.example: A learner asks which picture a partner means and the partner clarifies.
concepts.false: A request for clarification is evidence that language learning has failed.
concepts.note: Clarification can support shared understanding and learning.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A request asking a speaker to make an unclear message more understandable.
concepts.example: A student asks what a key instruction means before beginning.
concepts.false: Asking for clarification should be discouraged once a learner can chat fluently.
concepts.note: Repair strategies remain useful during complex learning at many proficiency levels.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Sufficient processing and response time after a prompt or turn.
concepts.example: A teacher pauses so a learner can formulate an explanation.
concepts.false: A delayed response necessarily proves that the learner does not know the answer.
concepts.note: Processing, language formulation, confidence and task demands can affect response timing.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Worry or tension associated with language use or evaluation that may affect participation.
concepts.example: A learner knows an answer but is reluctant to speak before unfamiliar peers.
concepts.false: Low public participation establishes low comprehension irrespective of anxiety.
concepts.note: Use several contexts and supportive participation opportunities before inferring ability.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Goals and willingness that influence engagement in learning and language use.
concepts.example: A learner practices expressions needed to communicate with relatives.
concepts.false: Motivation removes the need for accessible input and instruction.
concepts.note: Goals matter together with opportunities, resources and social conditions.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The age at which meaningful exposure to a language begins under a stated definition.
concepts.example: A profile distinguishes first exposure from the start of regular school interaction.
concepts.false: One universal age boundary predicts complete success or failure in all language skills.
concepts.note: Different skills and learning circumstances show different age-related patterns.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A view of language ability as varying by degree, task and setting rather than a single all-or-none state.
concepts.example: A learner understands lectures but finds formal writing more difficult.
concepts.false: Becoming conversationally fluent ends every relevant proficiency distinction.
concepts.note: Document abilities in specific domains and modalities.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Words and expressions useful for discussing curriculum concepts and relationships.
concepts.example: A learner practices compare, evidence and consequence in meaningful explanations.
concepts.false: Academic vocabulary is acquired completely through playground conversation.
concepts.note: Explicit encounters in reading, discussion and writing can be needed.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Language practices characteristic of a particular field of study.
concepts.example: A student learns how research-methodology reports describe variables and evidence.
concepts.false: One generic conversational test measures competence in every academic discipline.
concepts.note: Genres, terminology and reasoning conventions vary across subjects.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A conventional organization of an account of events, shaped by purpose and cultural practice.
concepts.example: A learner tells a familiar family story with an audience-appropriate structure.
concepts.false: All communities require the same story opening and order to communicate effectively.
concepts.note: Examine genre expectations without treating cultural variation as deficiency.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Discourse organized primarily to explain, inform or analyze a topic.
concepts.example: A learner writes a cause-and-effect explanation of a communication process.
concepts.false: Expository proficiency can be inferred directly from fluent casual conversation.
concepts.note: Academic explanation requires particular vocabulary, organization and explicit relationships.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: An interpretation drawn by connecting available information with relevant knowledge beyond what is explicitly stated.
concepts.example: A learner explains why a character left after reading contextual clues.
concepts.false: Inference is simply repeating the exact words of a text.
concepts.note: Check whether language access or background knowledge affects the apparent reasoning demand.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Combining relevant information from multiple parts or sources into a coherent understanding.
concepts.example: A learner integrates two classroom observations into one explanation.
concepts.false: Synthesis means copying one sentence without relating it to other information.
concepts.note: Language support can help learners express relationships among ideas.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A circumstance influencing whether learning in one language supports another.
concepts.example: Familiar concepts help when corresponding terminology and opportunities in the new language are provided.
concepts.false: Teaching a skill once ensures equal transfer across every language and task.
concepts.note: Similarity, proficiency, instruction and meaningful opportunity affect transfer.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Information and experience the learner brings to a task.
concepts.example: A child understands farming concepts well but needs school-language labels.
concepts.false: Unfamiliar English vocabulary proves lack of the underlying concept.
concepts.note: Separate what is known from the language currently available to express it.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Ongoing assessment used to adjust instruction during learning.
concepts.example: A teacher checks a supported explanation and changes the next learning activity.
concepts.false: Formative assessment exists only to assign a final rank.
concepts.note: Use findings to adapt support and identify next steps.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A stated target specifying useful language performance in a meaningful context.
concepts.example: A learner explains one cause-and-effect relationship with appropriate support.
concepts.false: A language goal should be chosen only from a fixed elapsed-time stage chart.
concepts.note: Choose targets from observed needs, curriculum and opportunities to learn.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A claim about processes such as inhibition, working memory or shifting rather than a general language skill.
concepts.example: A study tests task switching while controlling relevant group differences.
concepts.false: Better performance on one laboratory task proves general cognitive superiority.
concepts.note: Interpret measured outcomes narrowly and consider study design, variability and publication bias.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Expanded possibilities for relationships, participation and access through additional languages.
concepts.example: A student communicates with relatives and participates in more than one language community.
concepts.false: Social benefits require every bilingual to outperform monolinguals on cognitive tests.
concepts.note: Practical and relational value does not depend on a universal executive-function advantage.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The relationship between language practices and a person's sense of belonging and self.
concepts.example: A learner values both family-language connection and school-language participation.
concepts.false: All bilingual people necessarily have higher self-esteem than all monolingual people.
concepts.note: Identity experiences vary with recognition, choice and social conditions.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Learned and shared but variable patterns of meaning, practice, values and social organization.
concepts.example: A family explains its communication preferences and routines to a clinician.
concepts.false: Culture is a fixed set of traits possessed identically by every group member.
concepts.note: Cultural patterns change and overlap, while individuals interpret and practice them differently.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: An emphasis on beliefs, values, meanings and ideas in understanding culture.
concepts.example: An inquiry explores what respectful communication means to participants.
concepts.false: An idealist definition focuses exclusively on the physical objects a community makes.
concepts.note: Contrast an emphasis on meaning with an emphasis on observable material practice.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: An emphasis on observable practices, material conditions and artifacts.
concepts.example: A researcher examines housing, tools and daily work practices.
concepts.false: Materialist emphasis refers only to private beliefs without observable conditions.
concepts.note: Analytic emphasis differs from a claim that ideas or meanings are irrelevant.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: An inclusive treatment of cultural ideas, behavior and material expressions.
concepts.example: An account considers values, routines and the objects used in a celebration.
concepts.false: An omnibus account excludes behavior to focus only on abstract thought.
concepts.note: An inclusive definition spans several dimensions without assuming perfect uniformity.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The study of humans and human life across time and contexts through multiple subfields.
concepts.example: An anthropologist studies local child-rearing practices and their meanings.
concepts.false: Anthropology is restricted to judging which present-day culture is most advanced.
concepts.note: Describe and investigate human variation rather than ranking people on an assumed universal ladder.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Study of language in relation to social life, cultural practice and human experience.
concepts.example: A researcher examines how kinship terms express relationships and expectations.
concepts.false: Linguistic anthropology treats language use as disconnected from social activity.
concepts.note: It examines meaning-making within lived social and cultural contexts.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Recognition that cultural practices and meanings change across time and circumstances.
concepts.example: Families adapt communication practices after migration or technological change.
concepts.false: Authentic culture cannot change without ceasing to exist.
concepts.note: Change is a normal feature of cultural life, not proof that a community lacks culture.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Differences among people who share an apparent cultural or social affiliation.
concepts.example: Two Punjabi-speaking families prefer different ways of involving grandparents in appointments.
concepts.false: Shared language permits inferring identical preferences in all families.
concepts.note: Ask individuals about their practices instead of treating a group label as a complete personal profile.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A distinction between cultural practices and membership or identification with a nation.
concepts.example: Two people with the same nationality use different languages and follow different family practices.
concepts.false: Nationality identifies one uniform culture for everyone holding that nationality.
concepts.note: National affiliation and cultural experience overlap without being interchangeable.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A distinction between cultural practices and religious affiliation or interpretation.
concepts.example: Members of one religion differ in local customs and communication expectations.
concepts.false: A stated religious identity specifies every practice a person follows.
concepts.note: Ask respectfully about relevant individual practices rather than presuming uniform observance.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Recognition that socially constructed racial categories do not provide a complete account of cultural experience.
concepts.example: A clinician avoids assigning communication preferences from appearance.
concepts.false: Racial appearance reliably specifies a person's language and cultural values.
concepts.note: Self-identification and individual history are more informative than assumptions from appearance.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A form of group identification associated with shared histories, practices, ancestry or affiliation.
concepts.example: A person describes an ethnic identity alongside several language affiliations.
concepts.false: Ethnicity and first language have a perfect one-to-one relationship.
concepts.note: Ethnic identification and language use can change and need not map neatly onto each other.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: How people understand and express affiliation with cultural meanings and communities.
concepts.example: A student identifies with several communities and uses different resources in each.
concepts.false: Having several affiliations makes a person's cultural identity invalid.
concepts.note: Identities can be multiple, negotiated and context-dependent.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A reciprocal relationship in which language participates in expressing and organizing cultural meanings.
concepts.example: Kinship expressions and customary greetings convey social expectations.
concepts.false: Every culture corresponds to exactly one language with no internal variation.
concepts.note: Communities may be multilingual, and one language may serve many cultural groups.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The proposal that linguistic patterns can influence habitual attention or thought under particular conditions.
concepts.example: Researchers test whether language-specific categories influence performance on a defined task.
concepts.false: Language completely prevents speakers from understanding ideas lacking a single word in their language.
concepts.note: Distinguish influence claims from strong linguistic determinism.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The largely conventional rather than naturally necessary relationship between linguistic forms and meanings.
concepts.example: Different languages use different conventional forms for the same familiar object.
concepts.false: Arbitrary means speakers invent meanings randomly at every turn without shared conventions.
concepts.note: Conventional links are learnable and socially shared; iconic aspects can coexist with arbitrariness.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Organization of linguistic elements through patterns that contribute to meaning.
concepts.example: Word arrangement and grammatical markers help express who acted on whom.
concepts.false: Language consists of unrelated symbols with no patterned combinations.
concepts.note: Meaning depends on relationships and conventions, not merely isolated forms.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Organization in which units without meaning combine into meaningful units that can be further combined.
concepts.example: Speech sounds combine into words, which combine into larger expressions.
concepts.false: Every individual speech sound must independently carry a dictionary meaning.
concepts.note: Distinguish sound organization from the organization of meaningful linguistic units.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The capacity to create and understand new expressions using linguistic resources.
concepts.example: A speaker describes a new situation with a sentence never memorized before.
concepts.false: Language use is restricted to a finite list of memorized complete utterances.
concepts.note: Rule-governed combination allows novel messages beyond repetition.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Change in linguistic forms and practices across time.
concepts.example: New terms become conventional as technology and social activities change.
concepts.false: A language changes only when its speakers become careless.
concepts.note: Change is a normal linguistic process influenced by use, contact and social conditions.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Use of language to exchange meaning and coordinate social activity.
concepts.example: A child requests help, shares a memory and negotiates play.
concepts.false: Language has no use beyond communicating information to another person.
concepts.note: Communication is important, but language also supports thought, self-directed activity and imagination.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A natural language using visual and bodily articulatory resources with its own linguistic organization.
concepts.example: Pakistan Sign Language supports complex narratives and discussions.
concepts.false: All natural languages have sound as their primary required medium.
concepts.note: A vocal-only definition is too narrow; signed languages are fully linguistic.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The study of language meaning and use in context.
concepts.example: A listener recognizes that a question about an open window may function as a request.
concepts.false: The literal dictionary meaning alone determines every communicative intention.
concepts.note: Interpretation draws on context, relationships and shared expectations.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Learning language and social expectations through participation in community activities.
concepts.example: A child learns how to address relatives while joining family interactions.
concepts.false: Children learn language forms entirely separately from ways of participating socially.
concepts.note: Form and social practice often develop together through interaction.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Experience-related change in infants' sensitivity to speech-sound contrasts.
concepts.example: During the first year, responses become shaped by regularly encountered language patterns.
concepts.false: Every infant suddenly stops perceiving all unfamiliar-language sounds on the same birthday.
concepts.note: Development is gradual and experience-sensitive; no single month describes all contrasts or children.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Variation in the timing and size of early word knowledge across children and learning contexts.
concepts.example: A clinician considers words across languages, gestures and communication history.
concepts.false: One narrow word-count range at 18 months can diagnose every multilingual child.
concepts.note: Use appropriate developmental guidance and a broad profile rather than an isolated slide number.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Early short combinations often containing content words with some grammatical elements omitted.
concepts.example: A child says mummy go while beginning to combine words.
concepts.false: Two-word combinations normally begin only at exactly 30 months for every child.
concepts.note: Many children combine words around age two; timing varies and concerns warrant appropriate evaluation rather than rigid deadlines.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Continued growth of vocabulary, grammar and discourse through schooling and beyond.
concepts.example: A teenager learns specialized terms and new writing genres.
concepts.false: Every child learns exactly thirteen new words per day until age seventeen.
concepts.note: Vocabulary growth depends on experience and measurement; a fixed daily rate is not an individual milestone.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Study of relationships between language variation, language use and social life.
concepts.example: A study compares speech styles across settings and social networks.
concepts.false: Sociolinguistics investigates only errors made by second-language learners.
concepts.note: It studies patterned variation across speakers and contexts without assuming nonstandard means defective.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Language variation associated with social identities, relationships and practices.
concepts.example: Forms differ across peer networks and communication situations.
concepts.false: Every member of one social category necessarily uses the same forms.
concepts.note: Social categories show patterns and overlap; individual variation remains important.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Differences in language use associated with age, generation or life stage.
concepts.example: Youth slang differs from expressions preferred by older speakers.
concepts.false: A difference between age groups automatically proves permanent historical change.
concepts.note: Distinguish age grading from generational change using suitable evidence.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Relationships among language practices, gender identities, expectations and interactional settings.
concepts.example: A researcher examines variation within and across groups in comparable contexts.
concepts.false: Women naturally use complex grammar while men naturally use simple grammar.
concepts.note: Avoid universal gender stereotypes; roles, context and local patterns matter.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Social dimensions that can influence access, prestige and patterns of language use.
concepts.example: A study examines how institutional settings influence preferred variants.
concepts.false: Working-class varieties have less complex grammar and express fewer ideas.
concepts.note: Social valuation and educational access are not measures of a variety's inherent linguistic adequacy.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A variety associated with an ethnic community or identity in a particular context.
concepts.example: Some features are associated with a community's history and networks.
concepts.false: Every person assigned an ethnicity uses one identical ethnolect.
concepts.note: Association is probabilistic and negotiated, not an automatic consequence of ancestry.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A systematic group of English varieties associated with African American communities.
concepts.example: A grammatical pattern is interpreted using its community-specific distribution.
concepts.false: African American English is a pathological form of incomplete English.
concepts.note: Its patterned features require linguistic description rather than deficit assumptions.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A grammatical pattern in which multiple negative forms express a single semantic negation.
concepts.example: In an appropriate variety, he does not know nothing can express that he knows nothing.
concepts.false: Multiple negative forms must express a logical positive in every language variety.
concepts.note: Interpret the grammar of the variety; standard-English classroom conventions are a separate teaching issue.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Context-governed absence of an overt copular form in some language varieties.
concepts.example: A dialect permits a pattern such as you happy in contexts described by its grammar.
concepts.false: Copula absence permits deletion in every tense and every syntactic context.
concepts.note: Dialect rules constrain distribution; a short example does not establish unrestricted omission.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A socially regulated prohibition or sensitivity surrounding an act, subject or expression.
concepts.example: A speaker avoids a topic considered inappropriate in a particular gathering.
concepts.false: A taboo has the same meaning and force in every community and situation.
concepts.note: Norms vary across people, contexts and time, so identify the relevant local expectations.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Restriction or sensitivity concerning particular words or ways of referring to a subject.
concepts.example: A community discourages direct use of a term in a formal situation.
concepts.false: Linguistic taboo concerns only physical actions and never expressions.
concepts.note: Restrictions on reference can be related to social taboos without being identical to them.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A less direct or more acceptable expression used in place of a sensitive or potentially upsetting one.
concepts.example: A speaker says passed away rather than using a more direct expression for death.
concepts.false: Euphemisms have one permanently polite meaning in all contexts.
concepts.note: Audience, relationship and context determine appropriateness; euphemisms can also obscure important meaning.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A deliberately harsher or more disparaging expression for a referent.
concepts.example: A speaker chooses an insulting label rather than a neutral description.
concepts.false: Dysphemism is the usual term for making a sensitive expression gentler.
concepts.note: Distinguish softening, neutral description and deliberate derogation.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Meaning conveyed through resources such as gaze, gesture, posture, facial expression and spatial behavior.
concepts.example: A listener uses a gesture and facial expression to show uncertainty.
concepts.false: Shared vocabulary makes all nonverbal interpretation identical across cultures.
concepts.note: Nonverbal conventions vary and should be checked within the actual interaction.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The study of how space and distance are used and interpreted in interaction.
concepts.example: A clinician asks whether a seating arrangement is comfortable.
concepts.false: One fixed interpersonal distance is appropriate for every culture and task.
concepts.note: Relationships, setting and individual preferences shape comfortable distance.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Understanding gaze behavior with attention to the person's context and preferences.
concepts.example: A learner looks away while listening respectfully to an authority figure.
concepts.false: Reduced eye contact alone establishes poor attention or communication disorder.
concepts.note: Gaze is one contextual observation, not an isolated diagnostic test.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Communication across differing cultural experiences and meaning systems.
concepts.example: Participants check intended meaning when a familiar gesture is interpreted differently.
concepts.false: High grammatical proficiency guarantees success in every intercultural exchange.
concepts.note: Interpretation also involves context, expectations, nonverbal resources and repair.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Ongoing reflection on one's assumptions and openness to learning from others about their own experience.
concepts.example: A clinician invites correction rather than presuming knowledge of a family's preferences.
concepts.false: Cultural humility is achieved permanently by memorizing a list of group traits.
concepts.note: It is a continuing relational practice that recognizes limits and power differences.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Adapting professional communication and practice through attention to relevant individual cultural and linguistic circumstances.
concepts.example: An SLP revises materials after discussing their meaning and accessibility with a family.
concepts.false: Cultural responsiveness means applying the same stereotype consistently to everyone in a group.
concepts.note: Learn from the individual and examine how procedures may create barriers.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Evaluating other practices primarily through the assumed superiority or normality of one's own cultural standards.
concepts.example: A professional labels an unfamiliar respectful practice as deficient without asking about it.
concepts.false: Ethnocentrism is the same as neutral description of another community's practices.
concepts.note: Examine the standard being applied and avoid treating one's own habits as universal.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A generalized belief about a group that overlooks relevant individual variation.
concepts.example: A clinician assumes every family from one region prefers the same interaction style.
concepts.false: A group average establishes every individual member's behavior.
concepts.note: Group-level patterns do not replace individual information.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Respectful checking of how a practice or expression is understood by the participants concerned.
concepts.example: An SLP asks what a family prefers instead of assuming that a gesture is offensive.
concepts.false: A list of national taboos is sufficient to predict an individual's reaction.
concepts.note: Ask context-sensitive questions without requiring a person to represent an entire culture.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A systematic regional or social variety that may differ in pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar and use.
concepts.example: Two English varieties differ in verb patterns as well as vowel pronunciation.
concepts.false: A dialect is only an incorrect accent without grammar.
concepts.note: All speakers use varieties; standard varieties are dialects too.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A pattern of pronunciation associated with a speaker or group.
concepts.example: Two speakers share vocabulary and grammar but pronounce some vowels differently.
concepts.false: Accent covers every difference in vocabulary and syntax by definition.
concepts.note: Accent concerns pronunciation; dialect is a broader term.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A set of linguistic features associated with a speaker, group, activity or setting.
concepts.example: Regional English and the language of football commentary are both examined as varieties.
concepts.false: Only geographic dialects can be described as varieties.
concepts.note: The term is broad enough to include social and situational patterns.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A variety associated with a geographical area.
concepts.example: Forms are associated with a particular area while neighboring speakers share other features.
concepts.false: Every administrative district must contain exactly one dialect.
concepts.note: Linguistic boundaries need not coincide with political borders.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A variety associated with a social group or network.
concepts.example: A pattern is associated with particular social networks and class positions.
concepts.false: Sociolect means the personal language system of only one individual.
concepts.note: Distinguish group-associated patterns from an individual's idiolect.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The characteristic linguistic patterns of an individual speaker.
concepts.example: One speaker repeatedly prefers particular expressions and pronunciations.
concepts.false: Idiolect is simply the name for a language spoken by a nation.
concepts.note: Individual patterns reflect experience and context and need not remain unchanged.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Labels used in particular traditions for geographically associated speech varieties.
concepts.example: A lecturer uses regiolect while discussing regional variation.
concepts.false: A label such as topolect fixes one universally agreed boundary between language and dialect.
concepts.note: Terminological traditions differ; describe the variety and classification used.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A variety selected and supported for institutional uses such as education, publishing or administration.
concepts.example: A reference grammar codifies the variety preferred in formal school writing.
concepts.false: A standard dialect is linguistically superior because institutions support it.
concepts.note: Standard status reflects social processes and functions rather than inherent grammatical superiority.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A systematic variety lacking the same institutional standard status in the relevant setting.
concepts.example: A local variety has regular grammatical rules despite stigma in school contexts.
concepts.false: Nonstandard means that a variety has no consistent grammar.
concepts.note: Standardization and grammatical systematicity are separate properties.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Processes such as selection, codification, elaboration and acceptance that establish a standard variety.
concepts.example: Dictionaries and educational conventions support institutional use of a selected variety.
concepts.false: Standardization creates language where no grammar previously existed.
concepts.note: Communities already have linguistic systems before institutional codification.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Formal description or regulation of a variety through resources such as spelling conventions, dictionaries or grammars.
concepts.example: A spelling guide specifies conventions for published materials.
concepts.false: A variety without a dictionary cannot support meaningful communication.
concepts.note: Written codification is distinct from the existence of a language system.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Positive valuation explicitly associated with institutionally approved language forms.
concepts.example: A school rewards the standard form in a formal writing task.
concepts.false: Overt prestige proves that other varieties are linguistically deficient.
concepts.note: Prestige describes social valuation rather than structural superiority.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Positive value attached to forms expressing local solidarity or identity despite wider stigma.
concepts.example: Friends value a local variant that formal institutions discourage.
concepts.false: A stigmatized form cannot carry any positive value for its users.
concepts.note: Different audiences can attach different social meanings to the same feature.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A community linked by shared norms or practices concerning language use.
concepts.example: Participants share expectations about when particular styles are appropriate.
concepts.false: Every speech community uses one perfectly uniform grammar in every situation.
concepts.note: Shared norms can coexist with internal linguistic diversity.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A group whose recurring shared activity shapes practices, identities and ways of speaking.
concepts.example: Students in a debate club develop familiar expressions and interaction routines.
concepts.false: A community of practice is defined only by distant common ancestry.
concepts.note: Participation in shared activity is central to this analytic concept.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A pattern of social ties that can help explain language use and diffusion.
concepts.example: A researcher examines whether close local ties support a regional feature.
concepts.false: Geographic residence alone fully describes a person's social network.
concepts.note: Tie strength, density and relationships add information beyond location.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Language variation associated with activity, purpose or situation.
concepts.example: An SLP uses technical terms in a case conference and accessible wording with a family.
concepts.false: Register identifies only the region in which a speaker was born.
concepts.note: Situational variation is distinguishable from regional association.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Specialized vocabulary used in a professional or activity group.
concepts.example: SLP colleagues use technical assessment terms during a clinical meeting.
concepts.false: Using jargon necessarily indicates a separate ethnic language.
concepts.note: Specialized terms can increase precision among insiders while requiring explanation for other audiences.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A speaker's adjustment of linguistic features across audiences, tasks or levels of formality.
concepts.example: A speaker uses different forms with friends and in a job interview.
concepts.false: Shifting style proves that the speaker's home dialect is incomplete.
concepts.note: Speakers can expand choices without rejecting their community variety.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: An account of how speakers adjust communication in relation to others, including convergence and divergence.
concepts.example: A speaker adjusts pronunciation to signal closeness or distinctiveness.
concepts.false: Accommodation always means abandoning one's home language permanently.
concepts.note: Adjustments can be temporary and can express different relationship goals.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Adjustment making communication more similar to another speaker's patterns.
concepts.example: Two interlocutors gradually adopt more similar speech rates.
concepts.false: Convergence necessarily involves moving to a different region.
concepts.note: Interactional alignment can occur without migration or permanent dialect change.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Adjustment emphasizing difference from another speaker or group.
concepts.example: A speaker highlights a local feature to assert community identity.
concepts.false: Divergence means both speakers must become identical in their language use.
concepts.note: It can signal distance or identity rather than failure to possess a standard form.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A geographic pattern in which neighboring varieties are relatively similar while distant varieties can differ considerably.
concepts.example: Understanding is easier between neighboring communities than across the entire region.
concepts.false: A dialect continuum must consist of sharply separated uniform blocks.
concepts.note: Gradual variation complicates simple boundaries and binary language labels.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The extent to which users of different varieties understand one another.
concepts.example: Speakers from neighboring areas compare comprehension in natural exchanges.
concepts.false: Mutual intelligibility alone always determines official language status.
concepts.note: Exposure, attitudes, asymmetry and political histories can complicate classification.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A mapped boundary or transition associated with the distribution of a particular linguistic feature.
concepts.example: A map marks where a particular word or sound pattern is used.
concepts.false: One isogloss must identify the boundary for every linguistic feature.
concepts.note: Features have different distributions and may form overlapping bundles.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Unfair treatment linked to a person's language, dialect or accent.
concepts.example: A capable applicant is dismissed because a local accent is stereotyped as unintelligent.
concepts.false: Accent-based exclusion becomes linguistically justified when a variety is nonstandard.
concepts.note: Assess relevant communication demands without equating social prejudice with ability.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Ability to use resources from more than one dialect.
concepts.example: A learner uses a local variety at home and learns institutional writing conventions.
concepts.false: Learning a standard variety requires treating the home dialect as a disorder.
concepts.note: Teaching additional conventions can expand choice while respecting the existing repertoire.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Assessment that distinguishes community-appropriate forms from communication impairment.
concepts.example: A clinician checks dialect rules before interpreting a grammatical pattern as an error.
concepts.false: A monolingual standard-dialect norm automatically fits every dialect speaker.
concepts.note: Interpret forms in relation to linguistic background and use multiple relevant sources of evidence.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The relationship between habitual vocal characteristics and an individual's recognizable speech.
concepts.example: A familiar voice is recognized by resonance and other habitual features.
concepts.false: A temporary hoarse voice necessarily establishes a different dialect.
concepts.note: Voice characteristics, physical state and linguistic variety are related observations but not interchangeable categories.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A regional variety associated with the Shahpur and Sargodha area in the supplied regional discussion.
concepts.example: A survey records speakers' own labels and patterns around Sargodha.
concepts.false: Shahpuri can be established as the oldest Punjabi variety from its name alone.
concepts.note: Use cautious regional associations; historical priority and precise borders require specific evidence.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Labels associated with speech around Jhang and parts of the central-western Punjab regional continuum.
concepts.example: Speakers near Jhang use a local label for their speech.
concepts.false: The label proves one universally agreed oldest dialect with a fixed boundary.
concepts.note: Names and classifications vary across speakers and linguistic descriptions.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Regional labels appearing in discussions of varieties in the Rachna Doab and adjoining central Punjab areas.
concepts.example: A fieldworker records whether participants accept a local variety label.
concepts.false: All regional labels are equally acceptable to every community member.
concepts.note: Some labels carry social connotations; prioritize respectful self-identification and contextual classification.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A Punjabi regional label especially associated with the Malwa area of Indian Punjab.
concepts.example: A speaker identifies family speech with Malwa while living elsewhere.
concepts.false: A speaker's current address alone determines whether the family uses Malwai.
concepts.note: Migration and networks can carry varieties beyond their core regional associations.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A Punjabi variety label historically associated with the Doaba between the Beas and Sutlej.
concepts.example: A family retains Doabi features after migration from its historical region.
concepts.false: Doabi must be restricted to people currently living between those rivers.
concepts.note: Historical association does not exclude diaspora use or contemporary variation.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A set of related variety labels associated with the Pothohar and adjoining areas, with classifications that vary by source and community.
concepts.example: A clinician records whether a family identifies its language as Pothwari, Pahari or another label.
concepts.false: Pothwari is universally classified as merely an incorrect Punjabi accent.
concepts.note: Recognize self-identification and competing language-versus-dialect classifications.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A regional label associated with Dera-area speech, often discussed within Saraiki-related classifications.
concepts.example: A speaker from the Dera Ghazi Khan area describes the local speech label.
concepts.false: Derawali has one universally accepted classification as a Punjabi dialect.
concepts.note: Regional location and language classification are separate questions requiring source-specific care.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A language or group of related varieties associated with parts of northern Pakistan, including areas of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
concepts.example: A family reports Hindko rather than accepting a clinician's assumed Punjabi label.
concepts.false: Hindko, Kohati and Peshawari are interchangeable names for one uniform Punjabi dialect everywhere.
concepts.note: Respect regional and community distinctions; the handout's grouping is not a settled universal taxonomy.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Regional labels associated with the Thal area and neighboring speech continua.
concepts.example: A language profile records a family's preferred Thali label and actual communication patterns.
concepts.false: The Thal label fixes an identical language boundary for every speaker and feature.
concepts.note: Classification may involve Punjabi-Saraiki continua and differs by source and identity.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A local label used in the handout for varieties associated with the Chenab region.
concepts.example: A study documents how participants use the label rather than assuming it has one fixed definition.
concepts.false: The name alone proves a precisely documented mixture in equal proportions.
concepts.note: Treat the handout's mixture claim as a regional description requiring verification, not a quantitative linguistic fact.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Recognition of Saraiki as a named language and identity in descriptions of southern Punjab, alongside histories of competing classifications.
concepts.example: A clinician accepts a client's Saraiki self-identification and investigates relevant linguistic features.
concepts.false: Every southern Punjab variety must be relabeled Punjabi irrespective of speaker identification.
concepts.note: Avoid imposing the handout's broad Punjabi umbrella as an uncontested classification.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The extent of a language's active use and transmission within a community.
concepts.example: Children continue acquiring and using the language in everyday interaction.
concepts.false: Vitality is measured solely by whether a language has an official dictionary.
concepts.note: Transmission and use concern vitality; codification concerns standardization.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A sense of historical continuity and tradition associated with a language variety.
concepts.example: A community connects its language with a recognized historical narrative.
concepts.false: Historicity requires proving that the variety has never changed.
concepts.note: Historical identity can persist despite ordinary linguistic change.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Perceived or recognized independence of a variety from another linguistic standard.
concepts.example: Speakers and institutions regard a named variety as an independent language.
concepts.false: Autonomy is determined only by the number of vowels in a variety.
concepts.note: Social recognition and orientation contribute to classification alongside structural description.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: In the handout's classification framework, restriction of functions or resources relative to another variety.
concepts.example: A contact variety is discussed with reference to the range of functions it currently serves.
concepts.false: Reduction proves that its speakers have inherently reduced intellectual capacity.
concepts.note: Functional range is a sociolinguistic issue and must not be used to rank human capability.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The role of contact and resources from different sources in describing a variety's history or structure.
concepts.example: A linguistic description examines contributions from contact languages.
concepts.false: Any contact influence disqualifies a variety from being a language.
concepts.note: Contact is common; mixture is not a test of linguistic legitimacy or human worth.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Usage conventions that operate in practice whether or not officially codified.
concepts.example: Speakers share expectations for a form despite lacking a published style guide.
concepts.false: Linguistic norms exist only when a government publishes a grammar.
concepts.note: Community practices can establish effective norms without formal codification.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Beliefs and assumptions about languages and their speakers linked to social values and power.
concepts.example: A variety is described as intelligent because it is associated with a prestigious institution.
concepts.false: Language ideology is the same as a neutral inventory of vowel sounds.
concepts.note: Examine the social assumptions attached to linguistic judgments.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A pattern in which people use different forms at different life stages without necessarily implying lasting community change.
concepts.example: A youth-associated expression is reduced when speakers enter a different social role.
concepts.false: Any youth-adult contrast establishes irreversible language change.
concepts.note: Follow-up or historical evidence helps distinguish life-stage effects from change across generations.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Explicit or implicit decisions and practices governing language use in institutions or communities.
concepts.example: A school chooses languages for instruction, assessment and family communication.
concepts.false: Language policy concerns only officially printed national laws.
concepts.note: Institutional routines and unwritten practices can also regulate language access.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Efforts to strengthen a language's use, transmission and domains where it has declined.
concepts.example: Community members develop opportunities for children to use the language with fluent speakers.
concepts.false: Recording a word list alone guarantees renewed community use.
concepts.note: Documentation can help, but revitalization centers meaningful use and community goals.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A contested deficit label historically applied to apparently limited performance in two languages.
concepts.example: A reviewer replaces a broad deficit label with a detailed profile of opportunity, skills and language needs.
concepts.false: Semilingualism is a diagnosis established by mixing languages in conversation.
concepts.note: The handout lists vocabulary, grammatical accuracy, processing, creativity, functions and imagery; assess these specifically rather than assuming a deficient person.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A distinction between oral sound production and the broader organization and use of a linguistic system.
concepts.example: A person can have language competence through signing without producing speech.
concepts.false: Absence of spoken output necessarily implies absence of language knowledge.
concepts.note: Evaluate modality and the relevant communication system rather than equating speech with language.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Knowledge or use of multiple languages by a particular person.
concepts.example: One student uses three languages across home, study and work.
concepts.false: Living in a multilingual country proves that every individual uses several languages.
concepts.note: Individual repertoires and societal language diversity are distinct levels of description.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Presence and use of multiple languages within a society or institution.
concepts.example: A city contains several language communities and multilingual institutions.
concepts.false: Societal multilingualism requires every resident to know all local languages.
concepts.note: A society can be multilingual while some members use only one language.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: Exploring Linguistic Diversity.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: In Piagetian terminology, interpreting an experience through an existing cognitive scheme.
concepts.example: A learner initially treats an unfamiliar object as an example of an already known category.
concepts.false: Piagetian assimilation necessarily means abandoning a heritage language for a dominant group.
concepts.note: The handout's unqualified term needs context: cognitive schema use differs from sociocultural assimilation.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: In Piagetian terminology, modifying a cognitive scheme in response to experience that does not fit it.
concepts.example: A learner revises an earlier category after encountering a meaningful contrast.
concepts.false: Piagetian accommodation is simply changing seating distance for communication access.
concepts.note: Cognitive adaptation differs from clinical accommodations and from speech accommodation theory.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: bilingual lect _ 3.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A conventional expression presenting a general observation, lesson or piece of advice.
concepts.example: A familiar proverb conveys advice indirectly during a family conversation.
concepts.false: A proverb's intended application can always be recovered from literal wording alone.
concepts.note: Cultural familiarity, context and speaker intention guide interpretation.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A conventional expression whose overall meaning is not fully predictable from its separate words.
concepts.example: A learner needs explanation that an idiomatic expression is figurative rather than literal.
concepts.false: Translating every word individually guarantees the idiom's intended meaning.
concepts.note: Teach idiomatic meaning and usage in context instead of relying only on word-by-word equivalents.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: Meaning and social effect achieved through joking, incongruity or shared expectations.
concepts.example: A joke is understood within one group but needs explanation for an unfamiliar listener.
concepts.false: Failure to understand one unfamiliar cultural joke establishes language disorder.
concepts.note: Shared knowledge, idioms, context and relationships affect comprehension of humor.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A Punjabi regional label associated with central Punjab, including Lahore-Amritsar areas, and influential in descriptions of standard Punjabi.
concepts.example: A learner distinguishes a regional association from a claim that other varieties are inferior.
concepts.false: Association with a standard variety proves that Majhi alone is genuine Punjabi.
concepts.note: Institutional influence and regional identity do not invalidate other Punjabi varieties.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: An influential figure in American anthropology associated with historical and culturally contextual approaches.
concepts.example: An account examines a community's history rather than assuming one universal cultural ranking.
concepts.false: Boas can be credited as the sole first person ever to use evidence in anthropology.
concepts.note: Recognize his major influence without turning an honorific such as father of American anthropology into an exclusive historical claim.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The connection of culture with Latin cultivation-related usage, including colere meaning to cultivate or tend.
concepts.example: A discussion distinguishes a word's historical roots from its contemporary social-scientific definition.
concepts.false: The Latin root alone completely defines every modern meaning of culture.
concepts.note: Etymology can explain a word's history without replacing its current disciplinary meaning.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: multicultural lect  Basic Concept Cultural & Language L# 4.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: The connection of dialect with Greek dialektos, associated with speech or conversation.
concepts.example: A learner distinguishes the historical word source from the modern sociolinguistic concept.
concepts.false: The Greek word history proves that a dialect is linguistically inferior to a language.
concepts.note: The term's history does not justify modern social hierarchies or settle language classification.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

concepts.definition: A situation in which future use or transmission of a language is at risk.
concepts.example: Children have fewer opportunities to acquire a community language despite some adult use.
concepts.false: Dialects are inherently immune to language shift and extinction.
concepts.note: All varieties can face declining use; identity loyalty alone does not guarantee transmission.
concepts.referenceSection: Supplied deck: lect 5 Dialect.pptx; contextual further reading in the Reading guide.

sources.title: Baker & Wright (2021) — Foundations of Bilingual Education and Bilingualism, 7th ed.
sources.use: Recommended course book. Publisher-submitted announcement verifies authors, edition and scope. The complete copyrighted book was not accessed.

sources.title: Wardhaugh & Fuller — An Introduction to Sociolinguistics, 8th ed.
sources.use: Recommended textbook for variation, language and society. Official companion site verifies the edition; no claim of full-text review.

sources.title: Holmes & Wilson — An Introduction to Sociolinguistics, 6th ed.
sources.use: Recommended alternative textbook; publisher description checked for scope, not a substitute for access to the full book.

sources.title: Grosjean (2021) — Life as a Bilingual
sources.use: Authoritative further reading on real bilingual profiles; available publisher chapter descriptions were inspected.

sources.title: ASHA — Multilingual Service Delivery
sources.use: Professional guidance supporting the core principle that multilingualism is not a communication disorder and that service planning must consider the person’s languages.

sources.title: ASHA — Learning More Than One Language
sources.use: Accessible family guidance for multilingual development, language use and seeking support when concerns arise.

sources.title: ASHA — Cultural Responsiveness
sources.use: Professional reference for reflective practice, individualized inquiry and cultural-linguistic considerations.

sources.title: ASHA (2003) — American English Dialects
sources.use: Technical report establishing that dialect variation itself is not a pathological form of speech or language; use alongside contemporary individualized practice.

sources.title: ASHA — What Is Dynamic Assessment?
sources.use: Professional introduction to evaluating learning potential and supported performance.

sources.title: ASHA — Collaborating With Interpreters, Transliterators, and Translators
sources.use: Professional role distinctions and collaboration guidance. US-specific legal material is not presented as Pakistani law.

sources.title: Cummins (2008) — BICS and CALP: Empirical and theoretical status of the distinction
sources.use: Author’s discussion of the conversational/academic distinction; supplements the slide model without imposing rigid learning deadlines.

sources.title: Lehtonen et al. (2018) — Is bilingualism associated with enhanced executive functioning in adults?
sources.use: Meta-analytic review, Psychological Bulletin, 144(4), 394–425. DOI: 10.1037/bul0000142. Supports caution about universal cognitive-advantage claims.

sources.title: Rensch, Hallberg & O’Leary (1992) — Sociolinguistic Survey of Northern Pakistan, vol. 3: Hindko and Gujari
sources.use: Regional scholarly survey recommended for further investigation. Bibliographic record verified; the entire survey was not read. Precise regional borders and contested labels are not asserted as settled facts.
